summary: Proposes a plan for experimenting with ISO OSI network layer protocols over the Internet, and proposes an experimental OSI internet. Systems joining it must follow the agreements in this RFC. It requests discussion and suggestions.

eli5.summary: It invites people to test a different set of networking rules by running them on top of the regular Internet in a special club.

questions: how to experiment with osi over the internet
what was the experimental osi internet
what is eon experimental osi network
how to run osi over ip
subtitle: A plan to test OSI network layer protocols by carrying them inside ordinary IP datagrams across the Internet.

tldr.problem: The OSI connectionless network layer protocols needed large, realistic testing, but changing existing Internet routers to run them would be disruptive.
tldr.mechanism: Treat the Internet as a subnetwork: wrap each OSI packet in an IP datagram (IP protocol 80), derive the OSI address from the IP address, and simulate multicast with a small sublayer that keeps a cache of core systems.
tldr.outcome: The memo proposes an experimental OSI internet called EON, plus a UDP variant called EON-UDP, and warns that the methods are suitable only for limited experimental use.

today: The metadata for RFC 1070 lists its status as Unknown and records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The memo itself describes the scheme as a proposal for limited experimental use that requested discussion, not as an operational specification.

sections.title: Why Experiment over the Internet
sections.content:
The ISO OSI network layer protocols were in their infancy, and interest had grown with the US Government OSI Profile (GOSIP). The memo argues that testing should happen alongside the protocols' progress toward ISO standards, but that few implementors can build a large, varied, dynamic topology on their own.

Adding OSI to existing routers would be disruptive because the protocols and implementations were immature. The memo's answer is to treat the Internet as a subnetwork, the IP subnet, and to encapsulate ISO 8473 packets in IP datagrams. OSI protocols are meant to run directly over local links, and the IP subnet is used only to reach sites behind an IP gateway.

The experiment based on IP is called EON (Experimental OSI-based Network), and the one based on UDP over IP is EON-UDP. The memo includes a WARNING that the methods are suitable ONLY for experimental use on a limited scale and not for an operational environment.
sections.eli5: Few people have enough computers to test a new network alone. So everyone borrows the existing Internet as a road and runs their test traffic on it, without changing the road.

sections.title: Goals and Encapsulation
sections.content:
The goals are to help implementors test with each other quickly, using existing connectivity, without changes to IP gateways, with a logical topology that is easy to change and with minimal administration. Non-goals include arbitrary ISO-style addresses, a production environment for very many systems, and IP-to-CLNP gatewaying.

The whole OSI network layer PDU, whether an ISO 8473, ISO DP 9542 or IS-IS PDU, goes in the data portion of an IP datagram. If ISO 8473 fragments a packet, each piece is encapsulated separately. The intent is for OSI to fragment rather than IP, so that OSI fragmentation gets tested, but the destination must still support IP reassembly because the IP subnet may fragment anyway. The IP protocol field takes the value 80 (decimal).
sections.eli5: The whole OSI packet is slipped into the data part of a normal Internet packet, like a letter inside a bigger envelope. The outer envelope is marked with the special number 80 so the receiver knows what is inside.

sections.title: NSAP Address Format
sections.content:
The experimental internet is one routing domain with one address form, following RFC 1069. The address is built so that the IP address is embedded in it, which makes the mapping from an NSAP address to an IP SNPA address straightforward.

The 20-octet layout has the Authority and Format Identifier 47, International Code Designator 00, 06, version number 3, a Routing Domain Number assigned by IANA, padding, a LOC-AREA field, unused octets, the four-octet Internet address in octets 16-19, and an NSAP Selector in octet 20.

For LOC-AREA the memo weighs three options: IANA-assigned local areas, a single area with value 0, or an area derived from the Internet address. It prefers zero-valued local areas for now. Other address formats can still be routed through the domain by level 2 routers.
sections.eli5: The OSI address has the ordinary Internet address tucked inside it, so a computer can read the Internet address straight out of it, like finding a street number inside a longer mailing label.

sections.title: Simulating Multicast with the SNAcP
sections.content:
The ES-IS and IS-IS protocols assume a broadcast subnetwork with a multicast address for all end systems and another for all intermediate systems. IP does not provide that here, so a small sublayer called the SNAcP (SubNetwork Access Protocol) sits between OSI and the IP subnet. It caches the Internet addresses of core systems, those reachable in one ISO 8473 hop, and copies a multicast or broadcast packet to each cached address.

Before sending, the SNAcP prepends a 4-octet header: version 01, a semantics octet (00 not a multicast, 01 all ESs, 02 all ISs, 03 broadcast) and a 2-octet ISO checksum. On receipt it always accepts values 0 and 3, accepts "all ESs" only if configured as an end system, and accepts "all ISs" only if configured as an intermediate system.

ICMP errors such as destination unreachable, parameter problem and time exceeded are suggested to mark a cached address unusable and inform network management; source quench does the same with a timer after which the address is usable again. Other ICMP messages are ignored by the SNAcP.
sections.eli5: The Internet cannot shout to a whole room, so the helper layer keeps a list of friends and sends each one a copy. Each copy has a little tag saying who it is meant for.

sections.title: EON-UDP and Topology Files
sections.content:
Implementors without direct access to IP can use UDP instead. In EON-UDP the OSI packet goes in a UDP datagram to port 147 (decimal), with the SNAcP between UDP and ISO 8473. EON and EON-UDP systems do not interoperate directly. EON is the preferred method, and EON-UDP is only for those who cannot take part in EON.

The IANA keeps lists for each experiment. core.EON and core.EON-UDP hold the addresses of core systems as ASCII strings of the form A.B.C.D, one per line, with a pound sign starting a comment. hosts.EON and hosts.EON-UDP list participating end systems by name for the convenience of applications and people, and OSI does not use them. Sites join by emailing the IANA contact named in the memo.

The memo walks through a hypothetical topology of three universities and shows that a core system that changes role can announce itself by sending configuration messages, even while the IANA files are out of date.
sections.eli5: If you cannot open the big envelope yourself, you can use a simpler mail slot (UDP port 147). There is also a shared sign-up list of who is playing, kept by one person.

sections.title: Relationship to Other RFCs
sections.content:
RFC 1006 and RFC 983 run the OSI session layer and above over TCP/IP, whereas this memo runs the OSI network and transport layers on an IP internetwork.

RFC 1069 suggests using existing Internet routing and addressing in a gateway that forwards ISO connectionless packets. This memo does the reverse: it uses ISO routing and addressing in such a gateway. The addresses also meet the guidelines for the DSP part of an ISO address in RFC 982.
sections.eli5: Other documents carry the upper OSI layers over TCP. This one carries the lower OSI layers over IP, so it covers a different part of the stack.
